title: Reading the Intel Manual (part 2 of 2): ADD, Jcc, CALL, RET, JMP, CBW/CWDE/CDQE

questions.q: In 64-bit mode, what is the largest immediate that the ADD r/m64, imm form can encode?
questions.explain: The table says ADD r/m64, imm32. That is not a typo. ADD can only encode a 32-bit immediate, which is sign-extended to 64 bits before the add.

questions.q: An ADD instruction can encode a full 64-bit constant directly as its immediate operand.
questions.explain: ADD can never be encoded with a 64-bit immediate. The largest is imm32, sign-extended to 64 bits.

questions.q: You need to add the constant 0x1122334455667788 to RBX. Which approach works on x86-64?
choices: MOV the constant into another 64-bit register, then ADD that register to RBX
Use ADD r/m64, imm64 with the constant as the immediate
Encode the constant as a sign-extended imm8
There is no way to add a 64-bit constant on x86-64
questions.explain: MOV can load a 64-bit constant into a register. You can then use a register-to-register ADD, such as ADD r/m64, r64.

questions.q: How do the ADD AL, imm8 / AX, imm16 / EAX, imm32 / RAX, imm32 forms differ from the ADD r/m, imm forms?
choices: The destination register is fixed by the opcode instead of being picked by an r/m operand
They can only add to memory
They zero-extend the immediate instead of sign-extending it
They are only valid in 16-bit mode
questions.explain: These forms always use AL/AX/EAX/RAX, so they are less flexible. Their low opcode numbers suggest they date back to the original 8086.

questions.q: An ADD r/m32, imm8 instruction has the immediate byte 0x80. What 32-bit value actually gets added?
questions.explain: The imm8 is sign-extended. Its most significant bit is 1, so that bit is copied into all the upper bits: 0xFFFFFF80 (-128).

questions.q: An ADD r/m64, imm8 instruction with RAX as the destination has the immediate byte 0xF0. What does it do to RAX?
questions.explain: 0xF0 sign-extended to 64 bits is 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0, which is -16 in two's complement.

questions.q: Which of these operand combinations can ADD encode?
questions.explain: ADD's destination can be a register or memory, and its source can be an immediate, register, or memory. The two operands can't both be memory, and there is no imm64 form.

questions.q: Some ADD r/m8 rows in the opcode table are marked with * and a REX prefix. Why do these rows exist?
choices: The REX prefix lets the r/m8 operand reach the extra 8-bit registers added in 64-bit mode
They mark forms that zero-extend the immediate
They mark forms that only run on some vendors' CPUs
questions.explain: It is the same ADD, with a REX prefix so it can use the newer 8-bit register versions that 64-bit mode added.

questions.q: ADD's long opcode table boils down to a few operand patterns, each repeated for every operand size: immediate into the accumulator, immediate into r/m, sign-extended imm8 into r/m, register into r/m, and r/m into register.
questions.explain: The table looks daunting, but it is really five variations of one instruction, each listed once per available size.

questions.q: ADD evaluates its result for both signed and unsigned interpretations of the operands at the same time.
questions.explain: The CPU doesn't know whether the operands are signed. It sets the flags for both readings, and the code that follows checks the ones that fit its data type.

questions.q: After an ADD, which flag shows that the result was too big for the destination when the operands are treated as UNSIGNED?
questions.explain: The Intel manual says ADD sets OF and CF to indicate overflow in the signed or unsigned result, respectively. So CF is for unsigned and OF is for signed. The spoken paraphrase in the lecture swaps the two.

questions.q: After an ADD, which flag shows that the result overflowed when the operands are treated as SIGNED?
questions.explain: OF reports signed overflow. CF reports unsigned carry out of the most significant bit.

questions.q: After an ADD, what does SF (the sign flag) hold?
choices: The most significant bit of the result
1 if there was a carry out of the top bit
questions.explain: SF gives the sign of the result read as a signed number. It is set when the result's most significant bit is 1.

questions.q: AL = 0x7F. After `add al, 1`, which flags are set?
questions.explain: The result is 0x80. Unsigned, 127 + 1 = 128 fits in 8 bits, so CF = 0. Signed, 127 + 1 overflows to -128, so OF = 1. The top bit is 1, so SF = 1. The result isn't zero, so ZF = 0.

questions.q: AL = 0xFF. After `add al, 1`, which flags are set?
questions.explain: The result is 0x00 with a carry out. Unsigned, 255 + 1 doesn't fit, so CF = 1. Signed, -1 + 1 = 0 doesn't overflow, so OF = 0. The result is zero, so ZF = 1 and SF = 0.

questions.q: In the Jcc table, JE and JZ both have opcode 0x74. What does that tell you?
choices: They are the same instruction under two mnemonics, and the disassembler picks which name to show
JZ is the 64-bit version of JE
JE compares two operands while JZ tests one
One is the short form and the other is the near form
questions.explain: Both jump if ZF = 1. Different mnemonics can share one encoding, and the disassembler decides which one to print.

questions.q: JA and JNBE share opcode 0x77. When do they jump?
questions.explain: "Above" and "not below or equal" are the same unsigned condition: no carry and not zero.

questions.q: JE jumps when the zero flag is set.
questions.explain: JE and JZ (opcode 0x74) both check ZF = 1.

questions.q: In 64-bit mode, what displacement does a near Jcc use?
choices: An absolute address in an r/m64 operand
questions.explain: The manual marks the rel16 form as not supported in 64-bit mode. In 64-bit code a near Jcc is always rel32. The short form uses rel8.

questions.q: A short jump uses a signed 8-bit displacement. What range can it reach, relative to the next instruction?
questions.explain: A signed 8-bit value covers -128..+127, so a short jump reaches 127 bytes forward or 128 bytes back.

questions.q: About how far can a rel32 jump reach?
questions.explain: rel32 is a signed 32-bit number, which covers roughly plus or minus 2 billion bytes.

questions.q: When a Jcc is taken, how is the target address computed?
choices: The sign-extended displacement is added to the instruction pointer, which points at the next instruction
The displacement is loaded straight into the instruction pointer
The zero-extended displacement is added to RSP
The target is popped off the stack
questions.explain: The manual's pseudocode is tempEIP = EIP + SignExtend(DEST). In other words, add the relative displacement to the instruction pointer.

questions.q: The manual's Jcc pseudocode is written in terms of EIP, but in 64-bit mode the displacement is added to RIP.
questions.explain: The Jcc pseudocode is a bit out of date and has no 64-bit-mode case. Either way, the relative displacement is added to the instruction pointer.

questions.q: Every Jcc form uses a relative displacement. There is no absolute indirect Jcc.
questions.explain: All Jcc forms are relative. CALL and JMP also have an absolute indirect r/m form.

questions.q: A near CALL rel32's displacement is measured from which address?
choices: The address of the instruction after the CALL
The address of the CALL instruction itself
The start of the current function
questions.explain: The manual calls it a displacement relative to the next instruction. The target is the next instruction's address plus the rel32, sign-extended to 64 bits.

questions.q: A 5-byte CALL rel32 sits at address 0x401000, and its rel32 is 0x00000100. Where does it go?
questions.explain: The next instruction is at 0x401000 + 5 = 0x401005. Adding 0x100 gives 0x401105.

questions.q: A 5-byte CALL rel32 sits at address 0x401000, and its rel32 is 0xFFFFFFF0. Where does it go?
questions.explain: 0xFFFFFFF0 is -16 as a signed value. The next instruction is at 0x401005, and 0x401005 - 0x10 = 0x400FF5.

questions.q: The manual describes CALL r/m64 as "call near, absolute indirect". What does that mean?
choices: The value read from the register or memory operand is the exact target address. It is indirect because the address comes through that operand, not from the instruction bytes.
The target is a displacement added to RIP
The target is a segment:offset pair
The target is a 64-bit address hard-coded in the instruction
questions.explain: "Absolute" means the computed value is the address you go to. "Indirect" means you get it through a register, or through memory addressed as base + index*scale + displacement.

questions.q: Which near CALL forms are valid in 64-bit mode?
questions.explain: In 64-bit mode, rel16 is not supported and r/m16 and r/m32 are not valid. That leaves the relative rel32 form and the absolute indirect r/m64 form.

questions.q: What does a near CALL do?
choices: Pushes the address of the next instruction onto the stack
Sets RIP to the target address
questions.explain: A near CALL is a jump to the target that also pushes the return address, which is the next instruction's address.

questions.q: Far CALL, far RET, far JMP and call gates all depend on which mechanism?
questions.explain: The far forms work through segment selectors, and gates belong to the same mechanism. Operating systems use them. Ordinary user-space code rarely does.

questions.q: What happens to the extra bytes in a near RET imm16?
choices: After the return address is popped, imm16 is added to RSP. The bytes are discarded, not loaded into any register.
They are pushed onto the stack
questions.explain: The manual says "pop imm16 bytes", but nothing is popped into a register. The stack pointer just moves past those bytes.

questions.q: In 64-bit mode, how many bytes does RSP go up by when a near `ret 0x10` runs?
questions.explain: Popping the 8-byte return address adds 8, and the imm16 adds 0x10 = 16. 8 + 16 = 24.

questions.q: CALL's operation pseudocode in the manual runs about 10 pages. Which of these does it have to handle?
choices: Privilege level changes, such as going from user space to kernel space
questions.explain: Control flow is complicated. The pseudocode covers displacement sizes, privilege changes, CET, and processor modes. Floating-point rounding has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: Which JMP forms can you actually use in 64-bit mode?
questions.explain: rel16, r/m16 and r/m32 are not valid in 64-bit mode. That leaves three: short rel8, near rel32, and near absolute indirect r/m64.

questions.q: A 2-byte short JMP sits at address 0x1000, and its rel8 is 0xFE. Where does it go?
choices: 0x1000, back to itself, which makes an infinite loop
questions.explain: 0xFE sign-extended is -2. The next instruction is at 0x1002, and 0x1002 - 2 = 0x1000.

questions.q: In a relative JMP (rel8 or rel32), the displacement is part of the instruction's own bytes.
questions.explain: Relative displacements are constants built into the instruction. The indirect form gets its address from a register or memory instead.

questions.q: What kind of jump do you get from opcode FF with an r/m64 operand?
choices: A near absolute indirect jump: RIP is set to the address computed from the register or memory operand
A far jump through a segment selector
questions.explain: FF with a particular r/m encoding gives JMP r/m64. The address is calculated from the operand, and RIP is set to it.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a near JMP and a near CALL?
choices: CALL pushes the return address before changing RIP. JMP only changes RIP.
JMP can be indirect but CALL cannot
questions.explain: Both have relative and absolute indirect forms. CALL also pushes the next instruction's address so that RET can come back to it.

questions.q: How is a JMP rel8 displacement extended before it is added to RIP?
choices: It isn't added. It is used as an absolute address.
questions.explain: Sign extension keeps the value signed, which is why a short jump can go up to 127 bytes forward or 128 bytes back.

questions.q: What does CBW do?
choices: Converts a byte to a word by sign extension (8 to 16 bits)
Zero-extends a byte to a word
Swaps the two bytes of a word
questions.explain: CBW stands for Convert Byte to Word. It copies the byte's top bit into all the new upper bits.

questions.q: What does CWDE do?
choices: Sign-extends a word to a doubleword (16 to 32 bits)
Sign-extends a byte to a word (8 to 16 bits)
Sign-extends a doubleword to a quadword (32 to 64 bits)
Zero-extends a word to a doubleword
questions.explain: The family goes CBW (8 to 16), CWDE (16 to 32), CDQE (32 to 64). Each one is just a sign extension.

questions.q: What does CDQE do?
choices: Sign-extends a doubleword to a quadword (32 to 64 bits)
Sign-extends a word to a doubleword (16 to 32 bits)
Sign-extends 64 bits into a 128-bit register pair
questions.explain: CDQE stands for Convert Doubleword to Quadword, Extended. It sign-extends 32 bits to 64.

questions.q: The byte 0x9C is converted to a word with CBW. What is the result?
questions.explain: 0x9C is 1001 1100 in binary. Its top bit is 1, so the new upper byte is filled with 1s: 0xFF9C.

questions.q: EAX = 0x80000000. What is the 64-bit result after CDQE?
questions.explain: Bit 31 is 1, so it is copied into bits 63..32.

questions.q: The other sign-extension variants put their result in a register pair: DX:AX, EDX:EAX or RDX:RAX. Which instructions are they most likely used with?
choices: Divide instructions, which implicitly use those concatenated register pairs
questions.explain: Some DIV forms always use a concatenated pair such as RDX:RAX as the dividend. These variants put a correctly sign-extended value into that pair.

questions.q: The 64-to-128-bit sign-extension variant writes its result to which register pair? Use the high:low format.
questions.explain: RAX is sign-extended into RDX:RAX, a 128-bit value made of RDX (high half) and RAX (low half).

questions.q: For a SIGNED 64-bit division, why would code sign-extend RAX into RDX:RAX instead of just zeroing RDX?
choices: The divide treats RDX:RAX as one 128-bit dividend. For a negative value, the upper 64 bits must be all 1s to stand for the same signed number.
To save RDX's old value for later
Because zeroing a register is slower than sign-extending one
questions.explain: Zeroing RDX turns a negative RAX into a huge positive 128-bit number. Sign extension keeps the value the same. Try this by changing an unsigned long long division to signed long long and looking at the assembly.

questions.q: If RAX = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB (-5) is sign-extended into RDX:RAX, RDX becomes 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF.
questions.explain: RAX's top bit is 1, so every bit of RDX is set to 1. The 128-bit value RDX:RAX still equals -5.
